b96d7009-7d85-4be0-80b8-3e25514eed04.q: Why does Wells choose a first-person narrator with deliberately limited knowledge?
options: To allow the reader to know more than the narrator at all times
To describe the Martians' technology in accurate scientific detail
To mirror the experience of colonised peoples facing incomprehensible power
To show that the narrator is unreliable because he is lying

b96d7009-7d85-4be0-80b8-3e25514eed04.q: Which structural technique does Wells use when he switches the narrative to the brother's perspective for the London evacuation chapters?
options: He widens the scope of the novel while keeping the personal, eyewitness quality
He contradicts everything the main narrator has described
He removes the documentary realism that makes the novel convincing
He introduces a third-person omniscient narrator for those chapters

b96d7009-7d85-4be0-80b8-3e25514eed04.q: Wells grounds the novel in documentary realism by setting the invasion in real locations such as Woking and _____, making the impossible feel plausible.
The science fiction genre allows Wells to examine real-world issues including imperialism, class, religion, and _____ through a fantastical lens.
Match each narrative technique to its description.
right: Creates immediacy and identification but limits knowledge of events beyond the narrator's experience
A series of escalating incidents that strip away the narrator's confidence layer by layer
Use of real place names and precise technical language to make the invasion feel plausible

ff9c5e30-197e-4cc8-a60d-dd2f7e8d99fc.q: What does AO2 require a student to demonstrate in an essay on Pride and Prejudice?
options: A summary of the novel's plot in chronological order
Analysis of Austen's methods and their effects on the reader
A list of all the characters and their social positions
Understanding of the historical context of the Regency period only

ff9c5e30-197e-4cc8-a60d-dd2f7e8d99fc.q: Which of the following is identified as a common mistake students make when writing about Pride and Prejudice?
options: Embedding too many quotations into their own sentences
Analysing Austen's use of irony without naming it
Writing a thesis statement at the start of the essay
Retelling the plot rather than analysing Austen's methods

ff9c5e30-197e-4cc8-a60d-dd2f7e8d99fc.q: The WHAT-HOW-WHY essay model maps onto the three Assessment Objectives: WHAT = AO1, HOW = AO2, WHY = _____.
The quotation 'Till this moment I never knew myself' is linked to the theme of _____.
Match each quotation to the theme it illustrates.
left: 'Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?'
right: Class and social snobbery
Marriage as economic necessity
Darcy's pride and first impressions

27f6d1fb-5ec9-43d5-8c07-456920a9fc15.q: What type of exam question might require a student to analyse a given passage and then extend their argument to the whole novel?
options: A discursive question with no extract

27f6d1fb-5ec9-43d5-8c07-456920a9fc15.q: Which of the following is a key method associated with Wells that students are advised to analyse in their essays?
The Martians are ultimately defeated by bacteria — an ending Wells makes deliberately _____ to undercut any sense of human triumph.
The quotation 'slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth' refers to the Martians being destroyed by _____.
Match each Wells quotation to the theme it primarily illustrates.
left: 'an almost noiseless and blinding flash of light'
'never before in the history of the world had such a mass of human beings moved and suffered together'
right: Imperialism and the critique of British colonialism
The terrifying technology of the Martians
The collapse of civilisation during the London exodus

e33ce3a8-9152-4eb5-a136-76011cf978df.q: According to Mary Bennet's observation in the novel, how does pride differ from vanity?
options: Pride is concern for others' opinions; vanity is justified self-respect
Pride relates to one's own self-opinion; vanity is driven by concern for others' opinions
Pride and vanity are described as identical vices with the same root cause
Pride is always a moral failing; vanity can sometimes be virtuous

e33ce3a8-9152-4eb5-a136-76011cf978df.q: When Lady Catherine demands Elizabeth refuse Darcy, she uses the metaphor 'pollution' to reveal which attitude?
options: That Darcy is beneath Elizabeth's social standing
That Elizabeth's intelligence is a social threat
That she views class distinctions as a matter of biological purity

e33ce3a8-9152-4eb5-a136-76011cf978df.q: Austen argues that the Gardiners, despite their trade connections, demonstrate more refinement than many gentlemen — suggesting that taste and education are not the exclusive property of any _____.
Lydia's elopement with Wickham threatens her sisters because in Regency society a woman's _____ determined her family's social standing and marriage prospects.
Match each character or place to the theme or idea it primarily represents.
right: A physical symbol of Darcy's true character — taste without ostentation
Vanity and social anxiety driven by concern for others' opinions
The idea that refinement and good values are not confined to any one social class

8a9a5888-5fbd-4cf9-a171-1722c6a0b1cf.q: In genetic engineering, what is the role of a vector such as a bacterial plasmid?
options: It identifies and isolates the required gene from the donor organism
It removes unwanted genes from the host organism's DNA
It carries the isolated gene into the cells of the target organism
It produces the desired protein directly without entering any cell

8a9a5888-5fbd-4cf9-a171-1722c6a0b1cf.q: Which of the following is an ecological risk associated with GM crops?
options: Genes spreading to wild plant populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating herbicide-resistant weeds
GM crops producing less food than conventional varieties
Bacteria used in production becoming unable to reproduce
The cost of restriction enzymes making GM crops unaffordable

8a9a5888-5fbd-4cf9-a171-1722c6a0b1cf.q: Producers are at trophic level 1 in a food chain because they make their own food through _____, transferring energy from the Sun into biomass.
In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey fluctuate in a repeating pattern called the _____.
Match each ecology term to its correct definition.
right: All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area at the same time
The role of a species within an ecosystem, including what it eats, what eats it, and how it interacts
Organisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil

07659d4d-426d-4f45-91ec-a309a4499f72.q: What do the Martian tripod fighting machines primarily represent in the novel?
options: The failure of the British army to modernise its weapons
Overwhelming technological superiority, analogous to colonial military power
The narrator's psychological fear rather than a literal threat
Darwinian evolution leading inevitably to peaceful cooperation

07659d4d-426d-4f45-91ec-a309a4499f72.q: Wells uses the London exodus scenes — described through the narrator's brother — to show which of the following?
options: That the wealthy escape more successfully than the poor because of their resources
That organised religion provides comfort and guidance during the crisis
That the British army is ultimately successful in protecting civilians
That social hierarchies dissolve under pressure, with fine carriages no safer than carts

07659d4d-426d-4f45-91ec-a309a4499f72.q: The Black Smoke represents indiscriminate chemical warfare, while the Red Weed symbolises how colonisation erases _____ environments.
HMS Thunder Child, an ironclad warship, destroys two tripods before being overwhelmed — Wells uses this to contrast with the general sense of _____.
Match each Martian weapon or phenomenon to what it symbolises.
right: Technological dominance so complete that human resistance is meaningless
Indiscriminate chemical warfare and silent killing
Colonisation's erasure of indigenous landscapes, treating Earth as raw material

02adef1f-59ac-438f-9c2f-a4bf49628394.q: How does Wells use the curate's response to the invasion to critique organised religion?
options: The curate is shown to be heroic, proving religion can sustain people through crisis
The curate converts the Martians through prayer, showing religion's power
The curate's descent into hysteria and selfishness shows religion is inadequate in the face of genuine existential threat
The curate escapes the invasion safely, suggesting religion provides practical guidance

02adef1f-59ac-438f-9c2f-a4bf49628394.q: What does the artilleryman's behaviour reveal about his grand plans to rebuild civilisation?
options: His actions contradict his words — he drinks and plays cards rather than doing anything practical
He successfully recruits survivors and begins construction of underground tunnels
His Social Darwinist ideology is presented as a genuinely effective response to crisis
He abandons his plans only after the narrator convinces him they are unrealistic

02adef1f-59ac-438f-9c2f-a4bf49628394.q: The narrator begins the novel as a confident Victorian intellectual but ends it humbled and traumatised, demonstrating Wells's argument that _____ is the appropriate human response to our place in the universe.
The narrator's brother provides an alternative viewpoint of the London evacuation and is depicted as more _____ than the main narrator, rescuing two women from attackers.
Match each character to what they represent in the novel.
right: The failure of organised religion under extreme pressure — faith collapses into hysteria
The fantasy of Social Darwinism — grand plans for selecting the strong while doing nothing
Victorian intellectual certainty systematically destroyed, replaced by humility

7bd7bd2f-cdd1-4008-b5b3-b304f6b82034.q: How are the Martians ultimately defeated at the end of the novel?
options: The British army develops a weapon that destroys the tripods
The narrator discovers the Martians' weakness and organises a counterattack
The Martians leave voluntarily after achieving their conquest
They are killed by bacteria, against which they have no immunity

7bd7bd2f-cdd1-4008-b5b3-b304f6b82034.q: What does the artilleryman's language about selecting only the 'strong' and useful people echo, according to Wells?
options: Christian charity and the duty to care for the weak
Social Darwinism — the self-serving idea that only the fittest deserve to survive
Victorian socialism and collective ownership of resources
Scientific rationalism and the importance of evidence-based decisions

7bd7bd2f-cdd1-4008-b5b3-b304f6b82034.q: In the ruined house, the narrator watches Martians feed by injecting human blood directly into their bodies, literalising the metaphor that the coloniser _____ on the colonised.
Wells describes the curate's deterioration during the hiding scenes as representative of the failure of _____ under extreme pressure.
Match each element of Book 2 to the idea Wells uses it to convey.
left: The curate's collapse in the ruined house
right: Religion fails to provide comfort or guidance when civilisation collapses
Social Darwinism is a self-serving fantasy that justifies abandoning the vulnerable
Human survival was biological luck, not earned through heroism — humanity is part of nature

a6895ebc-0567-4a2f-ba99-2ed072170918.q: How does Wells use the Martian invasion as a critique of British imperialism?
options: He reverses the power dynamic so Victorian readers experience what it is like to be colonised
He presents the invasion as a natural disaster unrelated to political ideas
He shows the British army defending its empire against an alien aggressor
He suggests the Martians are justified because humanity deserves punishment

a6895ebc-0567-4a2f-ba99-2ed072170918.q: Wells positions humanity in the middle of an evolutionary hierarchy — neither the pinnacle of creation nor the most primitive life form. Which detail from the novel best supports this?
options: The narrator escapes the Martians using superior human intelligence
The Martians choose not to destroy all humans because they recognise human potential
The Martians are more evolved but more horrifying, while the bacteria that defeat them are less evolved but equally powerful
Wells argues that humans are actually more advanced than the Martians in moral terms

a6895ebc-0567-4a2f-ba99-2ed072170918.q: Wells explicitly cites the Tasmanian genocide to show that the Martians view humans as Europeans viewed 'primitive' peoples — as obstacles to be _____.
During the London evacuation, Wells shows class distinctions becoming irrelevant — the artilleryman's fantasy of selecting only the 'strong' satirises the ideology known as _____.
Match each theme to how Wells develops it in the novel.
right: Reversed so that Victorian Britain is the colonised territory, forcing readers to empathise with those Britain subjugated
Suggests humanity is not permanent or special — the Martians represent a disturbing possible future; bacteria prove that 'lesser' life forms can be equally powerful
Social hierarchies dissolve within days; survival depends on individual resourcefulness, not social position

586ff1e0-2102-485b-818f-b5f3caa766df.q: What does the crowd's initial reaction to the first Martian cylinder landing on Horsell Common reveal about Victorian attitudes?
options: Victorians were scientifically advanced enough to recognise the danger immediately
Victorian complacency — the assumption that Britain was invulnerable and could control any situation
Working-class Victorians were wiser than the educated middle classes about alien threats
Victorian society had excellent emergency protocols that quickly broke down

586ff1e0-2102-485b-818f-b5f3caa766df.q: How does Wells use the Heat-Ray to comment on real-world imperialism?
options: It represents nature fighting back against industrial pollution
It shows that Martian technology is ultimately no match for British courage
It is Wells's way of predicting the development of laser weapons in the 20th century
It mirrors how real imperial powers used technologically superior weapons against colonised peoples, making bravery irrelevant

586ff1e0-2102-485b-818f-b5f3caa766df.q: The white flag deputation approaches the cylinder to negotiate, but the Martians respond with the Heat-Ray — subverting the expectation of _____ and mirroring how colonial powers treated indigenous delegations.
The narrator describes horrors with clinical precision and scientific detachment, creating a tone that contrasts with the events and produces a sense of _____ irony.
Match each detail from Book 1 to its narrative or thematic purpose.
left: The crowd treating the cylinder as a spectacle
The Heat-Ray destroying the Surrey militia
right: Critiques Victorian arrogance and the assumption that Britain could negotiate with any force it encountered
Shows that technological superiority makes bravery irrelevant, paralleling how colonial armies overwhelmed indigenous peoples
Makes the impossible feel plausible and creates dramatic irony — the reader feels the horror the narrator suppresses

d285fe44-6dd5-4095-ac35-a27a2e444cc3.q: What is 'free indirect discourse' and how does Austen use it in Pride and Prejudice?
options: A technique where characters speak their thoughts aloud in long monologues
A form of third-person narration that gives equal weight to every character's viewpoint
A technique blending the narrator's voice with a character's thoughts, creating dramatic irony as the reader recognises Elizabeth's errors before she does
A method of narration where the narrator directly addresses the reader to explain character motivations

d285fe44-6dd5-4095-ac35-a27a2e444cc3.q: Collins's marriage proposal in Pride and Prejudice is an example of which narrative technique that Austen uses to reveal character?
options: Dialogue as characterisation — his pompous language condemns him without narrator commentary
Free indirect discourse — his thoughts are blended with the narrator's voice
Documentary realism — his proposal is presented as a factual account
Dramatic irony — the reader knows he will be accepted before Elizabeth refuses

d285fe44-6dd5-4095-ac35-a27a2e444cc3.q: In the opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice, Austen presents a social prejudice as a 'universal truth' — this use of _____ is her primary tool for social critique throughout the novel.
When Austen writes 'Darcy had never been so bewitched by any woman,' this is an example of free indirect discourse because we are inside Darcy's _____ but hearing the narrator's words.
Match each narrative technique to its effect in Pride and Prejudice.
right: The reader understands more than the character, seeing Elizabeth's misjudgements before she does
Blends narrator's voice with a character's thoughts, creating intimacy while maintaining analytical distance
Exposes the gap between social performance and private reality through satirical observation of class behaviour

de42c666-2a53-4680-a1c9-1c69e2e32abe.q: When was The War of the Worlds published, and what was significant about the historical context?
options: 1878, at the beginning of Britain's industrial expansion
1898, at the height of the British Empire
1914, just before the outbreak of the First World War
1867, the year Darwin published The Descent of Man

de42c666-2a53-4680-a1c9-1c69e2e32abe.q: What do the Martians represent as a product of evolutionary development taken to a disturbing extreme?
options: A warning that humanity will be destroyed by religious fundamentalism
A prediction that future humans will develop telepathy and abandon physical bodies
The ideal outcome of scientific progress — pure intellect without physical weakness
What humanity might become if intellect develops at the expense of compassion — technology without humanity

de42c666-2a53-4680-a1c9-1c69e2e32abe.q: Wells deliberately sets the Martian invasion in Surrey — the comfortable heart of middle-class England — to make the horror _____ and immediate for Victorian readers.

Wells was a committed socialist who believed Victorian class divisions were as destructive as any alien invasion — the curate's cowardice and the artilleryman's fantasies both satirise different _____ to crisis.
Match each Victorian anxiety to how Wells addresses it in the novel.
right: What if a more powerful civilisation treated Britain the way Britain treats its colonies?
If species can evolve and go extinct, humanity might not be permanent or special
What if progress produces power without compassion, making us more monstrous than improved?

0a9f80d5-5333-45f7-9d90-38255882269e.q: In genetic engineering, what is the role of a vector such as a bacterial plasmid?
options: It identifies and isolates the required gene from the donor organism
It removes unwanted genes from the host organism's DNA
It carries the isolated gene into the cells of the target organism
It produces the desired protein directly without entering any cell

0a9f80d5-5333-45f7-9d90-38255882269e.q: Which of the following is an ecological risk associated with GM crops?
options: Genes spreading to wild plant populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating herbicide-resistant weeds
GM crops producing less food than conventional varieties
Bacteria used in production becoming unable to reproduce
The cost of restriction enzymes making GM crops unaffordable

0a9f80d5-5333-45f7-9d90-38255882269e.q: Producers are at trophic level 1 in a food chain because they make their own food through _____, transferring energy from the Sun into biomass.
In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey fluctuate in a repeating pattern called the _____.
Match each ecology term to its correct definition.
right: All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area at the same time
The role of a species within an ecosystem, including what it eats, what eats it, and how it interacts
Organisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil
